meta.source: California K-12 Computer Science Standards (California Department of Education), reissued with framework alignment updates through Nov. 2023
meta.shape_note: Extraction matches the expected shape exactly: five strands, thirty core 9-12 standards (CS.1-3, NI.4-7, DA.8-11, AP.12-22, IC.23-30). Extended 2026-08-28 with the 6-8 band (24 standards: CS.1-3, NI.4-6, DA.7-9, AP.10-19, IC.20-24), extracted from the teacher's own CA CS Standards 3-12 spreadsheet (working-in-python/scratch/standards-source/, gitignored). Extended again 2026-08-29 with the '9-12 Specialty' set (30 standards: CS.1-2, NI.3-6, DA.7-9, AP.10-26, IC.27-30), marked core: False -- a separate, more advanced/specialized pathway defined in the same CDE document, not a deeper version of the core 9-12 standards. No 3-5 entries are indexed -- out of scope for this pass.

standards.paraphrase: Flowcharts and pseudocode let you design and check an algorithm before writing any real code.
A variable's name should say what it holds, since that's what makes the operations performed on it make sense to someone reading the code.
Real programs combine multiple control structures and compound conditions, and get built up iteratively rather than all at once.
Breaking a problem into smaller subproblems makes it possible to design, build, and review a program piece by piece.
A procedure that takes parameters can be reused for many different inputs instead of being rewritten each time.
A solution actually meets user needs only if you go get feedback from teammates and users and use it to refine the design.
Reusing someone else's code, media, or library in your own program is normal practice, as long as you credit where it came from.
Testing a program well means trying a deliberate range of test cases, not just the one you expect to work.
Building something as a team means splitting up tasks and keeping to a shared timeline, not just dividing the code.
Documentation is what makes a program usable, readable, testable, and debuggable by someone other than the person who wrote it.
A computing device's design shapes how easily people can actually use it, and proposing a change to that design is itself a real engineering task.
Building something that collects and shares data means choosing hardware and software components together, weighing tradeoffs like cost, speed, and size.
Fixing a broken computing system means working through a structured troubleshooting process, not guessing -- and a problem in one connected device can come from another.
The same data can be represented in more than one way, and choosing a representation changes what's easy to see in it.
Raw data collected with computational tools usually needs to be transformed before it's actually useful for answering a question.
A computational model lets you change one variable at a time and observe the effect, which is how you test what's actually driving a result.
Computing technologies that reshape daily life and careers always come with tradeoffs worth weighing, not just benefits.
Existing technologies can carry real bias and accessibility problems baked into their design, worth examining directly.
Building a computational artifact often means collaborating with many contributors, not working alone.
A license is a tradeoff between protecting a creator's rights and letting other people use and modify their work.
Making information public and keeping it private and secure are competing goods, and choosing between them is a real tradeoff.
Protocols are the agreed-upon rules that let messages actually get where they're going across a network, quickly and with errors handled.
Every network faces real security threats, and different threats call for different countermeasures.
Sending information securely usually takes more than one protective method working together, not a single fix.
Computing systems hide their internal workings behind a simpler experience for the person using them.
standards.scope_note: About hardware/device abstraction (e.g., a phone hiding its GPS hardware from the user), not software abstraction in code.

standards.paraphrase: Application software, system software, and hardware form layers that each manage their own part of getting a task done.
Troubleshooting a complex problem means researching, testing, and drawing on past experience with similar problems, and writing that process down so someone else can repeat it.
Networks have to satisfy real performance demands -- latency, bandwidth, throughput -- for the organizations that depend on them.
The internet's design, including how it looks up addresses and routes traffic, is what lets it scale and stay reliable.
Different security threats call for different defenses, and choosing between them is a tradeoff, not a solved problem.
Cryptographic techniques protect data in transit, and symmetric and asymmetric approaches trade off differently for cost and use case.
The same real-world thing -- a color, a character, an image -- can be represented digitally in more than one way, and converting between those representations is a normal task.
How data is organized and where it's stored is a choice with real consequences for cost, speed, reliability, privacy, and integrity.
Turning a data set into a visualization is itself a design choice that shapes what other people take away from it.
A computational model is only useful once it's been checked against real observations and adjusted where it doesn't match.
Solving a computational problem often means combining an algorithm you already know with one you design yourself.
Once a problem needs more than a handful of related values, a collection replaces a pile of separately named variables.
Different control structures for the same task read differently and run differently, and choosing between them is a real design decision.
A program built around events -- a button press, a timer -- responds to things happening rather than running start to finish in one line.
Breaking a big problem into smaller ones, each solved by its own procedure, module, or class, is what makes a complex program manageable.
A program built from separate, interacting pieces -- including code someone else wrote -- is organized by modular design.
Designing for a broad audience means building in a way to collect feedback from real users and revising the design in response.
Using someone else's library or code comes with license terms that limit what you can do with it.
A program gets better through repeated rounds of testing and fixing, aimed at more than just correctness -- performance and ease of use matter too.
Building something as a team, in defined roles, with shared tools, is different work from building it alone.
As a program's design takes shape, writing the decisions down -- in whatever form fits -- is what makes the process legible to anyone else who looks at it later.
Computing changes personal, social, economic, and cultural practices, not always for the better.
Bias built into a computing artifact, often from assumptions its designers didn't question, has to be actively tested for and reduced.
The same algorithm often turns out to solve problems in fields far from where it was first designed.
New technologies reshape social, economic, and political structures in ways worth examining critically, not just adopting.
Digital collaboration tools connect people across cultures and professions in ways that reshape how teams work together.
Intellectual property law cuts both ways for innovation: it protects creators, but it can also limit what gets built next.
A lot of personal data is collected automatically, without the person it describes actively participating, and that raises its own privacy concerns.
Privacy laws and ethics differ across places and contexts, and evaluating a policy means weighing its social and economic tradeoffs.
AI already sits inside plenty of everyday software and physical systems -- research one and explain how it's actually doing its job there.
Building a small AI-driven program that handles a simple task a living thing would normally do -- like navigating toward a goal -- is different from implementing AI theory from scratch.
Writing a real search or sort into a program to organize or retrieve data matters more here than choosing the fastest algorithm.
The same task written two different ways can run at very different speeds, and naming that difference with a time class -- linear, quadratic, log n -- makes the comparison concrete.
Different data structures trade off differently for the same basic operations -- inserting, deleting, modifying -- and picking one over another is a real design decision, not a formality.
Tracing how a recursive algorithm actually resolves means following the chain of calls down to a base case and back up again, not just trusting that it works.
A big, real-world problem usually decomposes into smaller pieces that already have a solution -- reusable code or a known procedure -- if you can spot the pattern.
A problem substantial enough to need decomposing is also substantial enough to justify building it from your own procedures, modules, or objects instead of one long script.
Pulling in a well-tested library or API instead of reimplementing its functionality is what code reuse actually looks like in practice.
Planning software for people beyond yourself means following an actual development-lifecycle process, not just writing until it works.
The same solution often needs to exist on more than one platform -- desktop, web, mobile -- and building it for more than one is the point here.
Reading someone else's code well enough to spot a security hole, show how a specific input would exploit it, and then close it is the actual skill.
A meaningful set of test cases covers ordinary behavior and the edge cases at the boundary, not just the input you expect to work.
Adding functionality to existing code means also tracking down what that change might break elsewhere, intended or not.
A code review means walking someone through your own code, and following along with real questions when someone else walks through theirs.
Building software as a group means actually using the tools that make group development work -- version control, a real IDE, documentation practices -- not just splitting up files.
Different programming languages fit different problems better, and being able to say why a specific language suits a specific task is the actual comparison.
A processor's logic gates -- AND, OR, NOT -- combine into higher-level circuits like adders, and that's the literal hardware carrying out a program's instructions.
An operating system's separate jobs -- managing memory, storage, running processes, controlling access -- can each be named and told apart.
Which data-collection tool you pick, and how carefully you use it, determines whether the data you end up with can actually support a real conclusion.
Software tools for analyzing, summarizing, and visualizing a genuinely large dataset are what make patterns in complex, real-world systems visible at all.
A model or simulation is only useful for refining a hypothesis once you've judged how accurately it actually represents the system it's standing in for.
Judging a computational artifact means naming both who it actually helps and who it actually harms, and proposing something concrete to fix the harm.
A technology that already reshaped some part of culture is still moving, and describing where it goes next -- and what that costs or brings -- is the forecast being asked for.
Access to computing resources isn't handed out evenly, and naming who actually benefits versus who's left out is the equity question here.
Real laws and regulations -- net neutrality is the classic case -- shape what software even gets built, and arguing both sides of that is the point.
A network's addressing scheme and its mix of routers, switches, and servers together determine how well it scales and how reliably traffic actually arrives.

The internet scales and keeps growing because of design choices baked into it from the start -- redundancy, open standards, and pushing key functions out to the endpoints rather than the middle of the network.
Defending against a security threat means weighing real tradeoffs, like a password policy that's easier to use against the cost of it being easier to break.
Cryptography, plus the certificate authorities that vouch for who owns an encryption key, is what actually secures a connection across the open internet.
